scenes.title: Start with a cost model
scenes.body: Count the operation that repeats. A loop that visits each of n items performs n visits.

scenes.title: One loop versus two
scenes.body: Two separate loops take about 2 n visits. Two nested loops over all pairs take n squared visits.

scenes.title: Describe growth
scenes.body: Big O describes an upper bound on growth. Drop fixed factors, but keep the dominant term. Predict how work changes when n doubles.

scenes.title: Begin with sorted data
scenes.body: Binary search requires sorted data and efficient access to the middle item. Compare the target with the middle value.

scenes.title: Discard half
scenes.body: If the target is smaller, keep the left half. If it is larger, keep the right half. Repeat until you find the target or the range is empty.

scenes.title: Count the halvings
scenes.body: A range of 16 items shrinks to 8, 4, 2, then 1. Doubling the input adds roughly one comparison. This is logarithmic growth.

scenes.title: Divide the input
scenes.body: Split the list into two halves. Keep splitting until each list contains zero or one item, which is already sorted.

scenes.title: Merge in order
scenes.body: Compare the first remaining item in each half. Move the smaller item into the output. Continue until both halves are consumed.

scenes.title: Combine the costs
scenes.body: Each merge level processes about n items. There are about log base 2 of n levels. Total work grows as n log n. A typical array implementation needs extra storage.

scenes.title: Choose a bucket
scenes.body: A hash function maps a key to a bucket. A lookup starts in that bucket rather than scanning the entire collection.

scenes.title: Handle collisions
scenes.body: Different keys can map to the same bucket. Chaining stores several entries per bucket. Open addressing searches other positions.

scenes.title: State your assumptions
scenes.body: With a suitable hash function and controlled load, operations are expected constant time. Bad collisions can make a lookup linear. Expected cost is not a worst case guarantee.

scenes.title: Make a request
scenes.body: A client sends a method, a path, headers, and sometimes a body. The server interprets these according to an agreed interface.

scenes.title: Return a response
scenes.body: A response contains a status, headers, and possibly a body. Success and failure should both have a clear, documented shape.

scenes.title: Trace one operation
scenes.body: For a to do list, the client requests the items. The server reads storage and returns structured data. The client renders that data and handles errors.

scenes.title: Keep a source of truth
scenes.body: Store the information that changes, such as a list of tasks and the current filter. Derive the visible list from that state.

scenes.title: Avoid duplicate state
scenes.body: A count of completed tasks can be calculated from the task list. Storing both separately creates two values that can disagree.

scenes.title: Make changes explicit
scenes.body: Use clear actions to add, update, or remove tasks. Recompute the view from the updated state. Test the action and its visible result together.

scenes.title: Check the shape
scenes.body: Validate required fields, types, lengths, and supported values when data enters your application. Give errors that help the caller correct the request.

scenes.title: Separate authorization
scenes.body: A valid identifier does not prove permission. Check whether the current user is allowed to access or change the referenced resource.

scenes.title: Keep storage consistent
scenes.body: Apply related database changes in a transaction. If any required change fails, roll the operation back. Report failure instead of partial success.

scenes.title: Separate code from data
scenes.body: Build a query with placeholders for values. Pass the values separately to the database driver instead of concatenating user input into SQL.

scenes.title: Bind a value
scenes.body: For a task lookup, keep the query structure fixed and bind the requested task identifier. The driver treats the bound value as data.

scenes.title: Constrain dynamic structure
scenes.body: Placeholders usually represent values, not column names. When a caller selects a sort column, map it through a fixed allowlist of supported columns.

scenes.title: Start with a visible model
scenes.body: Arrays make indexing, iteration, and data layout concrete. This example argues for starting there, then introducing objects once learners can explain the underlying operations.
